title: Thing on a Spring (C64) Tribute | 100% Procedural Remake with GPT 6 Astra
author: Disastrous-Round-150
selftext:
[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QiOnPawr\_do](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QiOnPawr_do)

A tribute to Thing on a Spring for the Commodore 64, rebuilt as a native Linux game with 100% Procedural graphics, music and sound effects.

Created with GPT 6 Astra, with creative direction by TEE JAY.

This video shows the complete automated playthrough: all 16 rooms visited, all five machine modules recovered, all nine puzzle pieces collected, and the goblin's final trap activated. The run starts from a fresh game and uses ordinary movement inputs, with no exploration assist, inventory injection, deaths or respawns.

The starting point was our earlier analysis of the C64 game. Recovered numeric room layouts, item positions and enemy movement recipes became the foundation for a new C++17 game. We reconstructed the gameplay, collision system, machinery, progression and final encounter, then built a completely new visual and audio presentation around that structure.

The result runs natively using C++ and GLSL/OpenGL. SDL2 handles the window, input and audio output. The game logic, renderer and synthesizer are custom code.

Everything you see and hear during gameplay is generated through code and mathematics:

• Characters and machinery built from analytic shapes and parametric curves.  
• Signed-distance shading, metallic surfaces, HDR lighting and bloom.  
• A chrome-and-lime spring hero with animated coils, compression and airborne extension.  
• Four robot enemy designs and animated factory mechanisms.  
• Parallax backgrounds, atmospheric lighting, particles and contact shadows.  
• Procedural vector lettering and interface graphics.  
• An original stereo soundtrack and synthesized sound effects.

There are no imported models, image textures, sprite sheets, external font files or recorded audio in the runtime. No game engine or C64 emulator is used. The factory follows the recovered room designs, while the default puzzle arrangement is reproducible from its seed.

The new soundtrack runs at 112 BPM, combining glass-like arpeggios, warm chords, bass, synthesized percussion and stereo delay. Lead phrases, breakdowns, fills and changing musical density give the longer playthrough more variation. It is a new composition; the original SID music is not included.

Sound effects use a queued, polyphonic synthesizer so multiple events can overlap. Springs, landings, footsteps, oil pickups, damage, doors, modules, puzzle pieces and victory have distinct sounds. Factory ambience and a rocket motor add another layer to the environment.

Building the complete replay also exposed problems that shorter tests missed. We corrected stair descent, doorway spawning, one-way platform collisions, shielded electrical fields and rocket movement against ceilings. Down + E now lets the player drop through thin platforms and conveyors.

The visual polish pass added rendering at the actual display resolution, smoother player and camera motion, clearer door prompts, more varied materials, quieter debris effects and distinct lighting for the assembly, foundry, dynamo and upper floors.

The finished game passed 96 checks, including the full campaign replay and sanitizer checks. The recorded route completes in 22,522 simulation ticks: 7 minutes 30.44 seconds of gameplay, ending with a score of 6,800.

The movie adds an introduction and ending for a total of 7 minutes 43 seconds. It was rendered offline at 1920×1080 and 60 fps, with synchronized 48 kHz stereo audio. The final soundtrack measures −16 LUFS with a −1.5 dBFS true peak.

This is an unofficial modern reconstruction and tribute. Its physics and final encounter use native reconstructed rules, so it is not a cycle-exact reproduction of the C64 original.
